subject: Pathology
summary: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant tumor of keratinizing squamous epithelium. Biopsy confirms SCC by identifying atypical keratinocytes with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls.

sections.p: SCC arises from squamous epithelial cells and is diagnosed by histology of a tissue sample. The biopsy shows malignant keratinocytes, intercellular bridges, and keratin pearls.

t.b: Shows cellular atypia and keratinization; a positive finding confirms SCC

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system, assessing tumor size (T), nodal involvement (N), and metastasis (M). Early stages (T1–T2) are localized; advanced stages (T3–T4, N+, M+) carry poorer prognosis.

t.b: Defines T stage and nodal status; helps plan surgery or radiation

sections.p: SCC is driven by cumulative DNA damage from carcinogens. The most common causes are ultraviolet radiation, tobacco smoke, and human papillomavirus (HPV).

t.b: Detects high‑risk HPV types; positive suggests viral etiology

sections.p: Patients often report a non-healing ulcer, indurated plaque, or mass. Symptoms vary by site: skin lesions may be painless; oral SCC can cause pain, dysphagia, or bleeding.

t.b: Identifies lesion characteristics and regional lymphadenopathy

sections.p: Beyond biopsy, investigations assess extent and rule out mimics. Imaging, endoscopy, and laboratory tests guide staging and treatment.

t.b: Detects distant metastasis; a negative result supports localized disease
Evaluates anemia or infection that may complicate treatment
HIV status influences treatment tolerance and prognosis

sections.p: Rapid growth, ulceration, pain, or regional lymph node enlargement suggest aggressive disease. Complications include airway obstruction, bleeding, and secondary infection.

t.b: Red flag if lesion >2 cm or painful

sections.p: Treatment is tailored to stage and patient fitness. Options include surgery, radiation, or combined modality. Adjunctive care addresses nutrition, pain, and infection.
b: Radiation therapy for unresectable or high‑risk lesions

t.b: Ensures complete removal; positive margins warrant re-excision or radiation

sections.p: Regular surveillance detects recurrence early. Prevention focuses on sun protection, smoking cessation, and HPV vaccination.

t.b: Monitors for new lesions or recurrence

sections.p: Benign keratoses, basal cell carcinoma, and actinic keratosis can mimic SCC. Histology distinguishes them by cellular atypia and invasion depth.

t.b: Differentiates based on invasion pattern and cell morphology

sections.p: A biopsy may miss invasive foci if sampling is superficial. Imaging may underestimate nodal disease in early stages.

t.b: If clinical suspicion remains high despite negative initial sample

faq.q: Can SCC be cured if caught early?
faq.a: Yes, early-stage SCC with clear surgical margins has a high cure rate.

faq.q: Is HPV vaccination useful for SCC prevention?
faq.a: HPV vaccination reduces risk of SCC in anogenital and oropharyngeal sites.

faq.q: What if a biopsy is unavailable?
faq.a: Clinical diagnosis with imaging and referral for biopsy is essential; empiric treatment is not advised.
